vignette:
She is 67 years old, widowed, and has spent most of her adult life working as a database administrator, a job that suits her careful mind and preference for systems that behave predictably. When she first begins to talk about her history, she does so in a measured way, as if organizing events into neat columns might make them more bearable. She is from Oceania and speaks with quiet pride about the steadiness she has built for herself over the years, though it takes little time for that steadiness to reveal how hard-won it has been.

She describes meeting her former romantic partner in adulthood, at a time when she believed she had finally found companionship that felt safe. At first he is attentive and persuasive, and she recalls wanting to trust the version of him that was warm and charming in public. The violence begins gradually, then escalates. He grabs her during arguments, shoves her into walls, and once leaves a bruise across her upper arm that she hides beneath long sleeves at work. She tells herself, at first, that it is stress, that he is under pressure, that if she is quieter, more careful, more accommodating, the anger will pass. Instead, the home she shares with him becomes a place where she is always listening for the sound of his footsteps, the tone of his voice, the click of a door closing too hard.

She learns to scan rooms automatically. She notices exits, weighs the distance to the car, keeps her keys in her hand before she is ready to leave. Even now, decades later, she sits with her back to a wall whenever possible and becomes visibly tense if someone stands too close behind her. She says she never used to be this way; she once walked through life assuming most people meant well. The abuse changes that. She begins sleeping lightly, waking at the slightest movement in the house. On the worst nights she lies awake and rehearses what she might say if he starts again, though she already knows words do little to stop him. Sometimes she drifts off and wakes with her heart pounding, disoriented, certain for a moment that he is in the room.

At work, she keeps her composure and continues to perform with great precision. In her role as a database administrator, she manages problems that demand calm under pressure, and colleagues often see only her competence. She prefers this. The predictability of systems feels safer than people. But the concentration that once came easily is now interrupted by flashes of memory. A raised voice in the office, a colleague slamming a drawer, even an unexpected email notification can make her stomach drop. She feels her shoulders tighten and her thoughts scatter. She catches herself rereading the same line on the screen because part of her mind has gone somewhere else entirely, back into the house where she used to brace for impact.

The relationship ends, though not cleanly. She leaves and returns more than once, pulled by fear, hope, financial concerns, and the shame of believing she should have recognized the danger sooner. When she finally separates from him for good, she expects relief to arrive quickly. Instead, the fear seems to follow her. She has intrusive images of his face when angry, or of his hand coming up before the blow lands. Certain smells, the sound of heavy breathing, the feel of a slammed door all bring a rush of dread so immediate that she has to steady herself by naming objects in the room. She dislikes crowded places and avoids social gatherings where she cannot easily leave. She says she used to enjoy community events and visiting friends, but now she often declines invitations, telling people she is tired or busy.

Her widowed status carries its own layer of loneliness. After her husband dies, she finds herself more vulnerable to the old memories, as if the quiet left by his absence gives more room for the past to enter. Still, she continues to live carefully and independently. She keeps her home orderly, checks locks more than once, and leaves lights on in rooms she is not using. She tells herself these habits are practical, but she also knows they are part of how she tries to feel prepared for danger that no longer belongs in her present.

In sessions, she speaks of grief not only for what happened but for who she was before it. She feels anger at how long she endured the abuse and sadness for the years spent afraid in her own home. At times she becomes tearful while describing how ordinary life can still feel interrupted by the body’s old alarms. Yet there are signs of resilience in the way she tells her story: with clarity, with persistence, and with a quiet determination to keep going even when her mind returns, uninvited, to the past.
